If a job is tough, dirty, or odd hours, locals don’t always line up, and immigrants often step in. I’m fine with that when it’s above board: same pay for the same work, proper visas, safety standards, and proof the employer tried to hire locally at a fair wage. What I push back on is using migrant labor as a shortcut to keep wages low. If there’s truly a shortage, raise pay, improve conditions, offer training, then bring in workers to fill the gaps.

Cultural diversity and vitality: You can feel the energy—new foods, festivals, shops, and different ways of looking at problems. That can be a plus for a town. The part that needs care is pace and connection. If change happens faster than people can get to know each other, you get friction. I like practical steps: English classes, civics and safety orientation, and chances to mix—school events, block parties, rec leagues—so we’re not living in silos. Shared basics matter: a common language in the commons, respect for local rules, and willingness to pitch in.

Security concerns: Wanting secure borders and solid vetting is reasonable. Most immigrants I know are working hard and keeping their heads down. From the reports I trust, immigration doesn’t automatically spike crime, but local problems can crop up if housing is overcrowded or if shady employers and traffickers are involved. So aim at the real risks: strong border and port security, smart screening, and going after exploitation—labor brokers, gangs, anyone preying on people. Also make it safe for immigrant communities to report crimes without fear; that helps everyone.

Humanitarian perspective: I respect the idea that America offers refuge. If someone’s fleeing war or persecution, we should have a fair, rigorous process to give them a shot. But don’t dump the costs on the same working‑class towns already stretched. Pair admissions with funding for housing, schools, health care, and job placement; spread resettlement so one ZIP code doesn’t shoulder it all. Sponsors and community groups can help with the basics—English, paperwork, first jobs—so folks get on their feet and contribute.

Employment and income fears: That’s the sore spot for people like me. If you’re on the bottom rung, a flood of cheaper labor can feel like the floor dropping out. Sometimes the problem isn’t the workers; it’s employers gaming the system. The fix is enforcement and standards: prevailing‑wage rules on visas, E‑Verify with teeth, big penalties for wage theft and misclassification, and backing for unions or worker councils so nobody’s undercut. Add training and apprenticeships so locals can move into the jobs that actually exist.

Where I want more evidence or dialogue:
- Local wage and hiring data: Are employers truly short of workers, or just not offering enough?
- Housing and school capacity: Can the area absorb new arrivals without overcrowding?
- Crime trends by community: Not headlines—real numbers and context.
- Fiscal impact: What’s the net on taxes paid versus services used, and how does it vary by place?
- Integration metrics: English proficiency, job progression, civic participation—are we setting people up to belong?

Who should be at the table: line workers, small business owners, teachers, cops, nurses, and immigrant families themselves. They see the daily realities. If you listen to those voices, you usually end up with middle‑lane solutions—legal pathways tied to demand, firm labor standards, strong borders and vetting, and real support for communities absorbing change.

Bottom line, a lot of these viewpoints have a piece of truth. The trick is not to turn them into all‑or‑nothing camps. We can value contributions, keep the country safe, live up to our humanitarian values, and protect local paychecks—if we stick to fair rules and keep talking to each other instead of shouting past each other.

We follow public health guidance, avoid gossip, and ask if there are practical ways to help—groceries dropped off, flexible timing at events, that sort of thing. People feel comfortable when they’re not singled out or judged, and when neighbors trust that we’re handling things calmly and responsibly.

Differences in race, religion, language, or who people love don’t bother me. Comfort there comes from everyday courtesy: learn names, pronounce them right, don’t make assumptions, and be patient with language. If someone’s English is limited, we slow down, use simple words, maybe a translation app, and keep a sense of humor. For religious practices, we’re mindful about scheduling and space—no one gets special privilege, but no one gets shut out either. And family setup is none of my business; we look at conduct, not labels. If you treat people decent and pitch in, you belong.

Where more communication and tolerance are needed is mostly in the gray areas—noise, parking, cultural habits that look different at first, and the tension that comes when folks feel their routines are getting bumped. Reasons are human: change can feel fast, people worry about safety and fairness, and sometimes pride gets in the way. Talking early helps. I find it works to knock on a door and say, “Hey, can we figure out a fix that works for both of us?” rather than leading with a complaint. Ask questions, assume good intent, and use “here’s what I’m noticing” instead of “you always.” If that doesn’t stick, we bring it to the group and set clear, written expectations so nobody feels singled out.

Bottom line, the kind of interaction that makes people comfortable is steady, neighborly contact with clear boundaries: greet each other, share small favors, listen before judging, and keep the commons safe and tidy. Show up for mulch day, potlucks, and storm cleanups. Give grace for differences, but draw the line at behavior that puts others at risk. That’s how you build a place where everyone can breathe easy and belong.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character09_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are tight, fairness means the folks who’ve been carrying the load here—paying taxes, raising kids, keeping the lights on—get the first crack at openings. No cutting in line. You post the job locally, offer a decent wage, and give residents a real shot. If after a fair try the spot still can’t be filled, then you widen the circle and bring in workers through the proper channels.

A big piece of balance is making sure employers can’t play games. Same pay for the same work, same safety standards, same benefits—no under‑the‑table hires, no misclassifying people to dodge overtime. If migrant workers are needed, fine, but they shouldn’t be used to drive a race to the bottom. Hold companies to proof they tried to hire locally at a fair wage before tapping outside labor.

We should fund training so locals can step into the jobs that exist—apprenticeships, community college certificates, paid on‑the‑job learning. Tie some of that funding to the sectors bringing in workers, so we’re growing local talent alongside filling immediate gaps. And if we do bring in workers, make sure there’s a plan for housing and schools so the strain doesn’t land on the same working families already stretched thin.

For roles that are seasonal or highly specialized—harvest crews, elder care, certain construction trades—I’m fine with targeted visas linked to real demand, with tight oversight on recruiters and labor brokers. Put teeth in the rules: big penalties for anyone exploiting workers or stiffing them on wages. Good for the migrants, good for the locals, because clean competition beats shady shortcuts.

I also expect anyone coming in to play by the same basics: follow the law, pay taxes, learn the ropes of the community—English classes, safety training, the civic stuff. That’s how belonging starts. On the flip side, we shouldn’t turn neighbors into enemies. Most folks—local or migrant—just want a fair shot. The real squeeze usually comes from the top when companies chase the cheapest possible labor.

On the undocumented piece, I don’t think looking the other way is fair. If someone’s been here a long time, working and keeping their nose clean, there should be a tough but doable path to get right—background checks, fines, learning English, then getting in line like anyone else. For people gaming the system or exploiting workers, go after them hard—especially the employers enabling it.

So, balance to me is: locals get first dibs, migrants come in where there’s a proven need, everyone plays by the same rules and wages, and we invest in the community so the load is shared. That’s a setup where fairness isn’t just a slogan—it shows up in paychecks, job postings, and how we treat each other on the job site.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character09_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I try to sort it into buckets and keep it grounded in what people actually feel on the ground.

Labor shortages: That’s a real thing in certain sectors—farm work, elder care, food processing, some construction trades. If a job is tough, dirty, or odd hours, locals don’t always line up, and immigrants often step in. I’m fine with that when it’s above board: same pay for the same work, proper visas, safety standards, and proof the employer tried to hire locally at a fair wage. What I push back on is using migrant labor as a shortcut to keep wages low. If there’s truly a shortage, raise pay, improve conditions, offer training, then bring in workers to fill the gaps.

Cultural diversity and vitality: You can feel the energy—new foods, festivals, shops, and different ways of looking at problems. That can be a plus for a town. The part that needs care is pace and connection. If change happens faster than people can get to know each other, you get friction. I like practical steps: English classes, civics and safety orientation, and chances to mix—school events, block parties, rec leagues—so we’re not living in silos. Shared basics matter: a common language in the commons, respect for local rules, and willingness to pitch in.

Security concerns: Wanting secure borders and solid vetting is reasonable. Most immigrants I know are working hard and keeping their heads down. From the reports I trust, immigration doesn’t automatically spike crime, but local problems can crop up if housing is overcrowded or if shady employers and traffickers are involved. So aim at the real risks: strong border and port security, smart screening, and going after exploitation—labor brokers, gangs, anyone preying on people. Also make it safe for immigrant communities to report crimes without fear; that helps everyone.

Humanitarian perspective: I respect the idea that America offers refuge. If someone’s fleeing war or persecution, we should have a fair, rigorous process to give them a shot. But don’t dump the costs on the same working‑class towns already stretched. Pair admissions with funding for housing, schools, health care, and job placement; spread resettlement so one ZIP code doesn’t shoulder it all. Sponsors and community groups can help with the basics—English, paperwork, first jobs—so folks get on their feet and contribute.

Employment and income fears: That’s the sore spot for people like me. If you’re on the bottom rung, a flood of cheaper labor can feel like the floor dropping out. Sometimes the problem isn’t the workers; it’s employers gaming the system. The fix is enforcement and standards: prevailing‑wage rules on visas, E‑Verify with teeth, big penalties for wage theft and misclassification, and backing for unions or worker councils so nobody’s undercut. Add training and apprenticeships so locals can move into the jobs that actually exist.

Where I want more evidence or dialogue:
- Local wage and hiring data: Are employers truly short of workers, or just not offering enough?
- Housing and school capacity: Can the area absorb new arrivals without overcrowding?
- Crime trends by community: Not headlines—real numbers and context.
- Fiscal impact: What’s the net on taxes paid versus services used, and how does it vary by place?
- Integration metrics: English proficiency, job progression, civic participation—are we setting people up to belong?

Who should be at the table: line workers, small business owners, teachers, cops, nurses, and immigrant families themselves. They see the daily realities. If you listen to those voices, you usually end up with middle‑lane solutions—legal pathways tied to demand, firm labor standards, strong borders and vetting, and real support for communities absorbing change.

Bottom line, a lot of these viewpoints have a piece of truth. The trick is not to turn them into all‑or‑nothing camps. We can value contributions, keep the country safe, live up to our humanitarian values, and protect local paychecks—if we stick to fair rules and keep talking to each other instead of shouting past each other.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character09_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go with wide‑open borders or a hard shut door. The middle lane makes the most sense: admit people based on real job demand, with clear numerical limits, strong enforcement, and solid support for communities and workers. Here’s the mix I’d back and why:

- Job‑demand visas with guardrails:
  - Employers have to post locally first at a fair, prevailing wage, offer training, and show they couldn’t fill the job.
  - Same pay, same safety, same benefits for everyone doing the job.
  - Give workers visa portability so they can change employers and aren’t trapped in bad situations.

- Numerical limits that move with reality:
  - Set annual caps by category—skilled, seasonal, family reunification, refugees—based on labor data and community capacity (housing, schools).
  - Review and adjust yearly, publish the numbers, and keep it predictable.

- Locals‑first investments:
  - Fund apprenticeships, community college certificates, and paid on‑the‑job training so residents can step into the jobs we’re bringing people in for.
  - Make employers pay into a training and community impact fund if they use visa programs.

- Strong enforcement focused on the real cheaters:
  - Mandatory E‑Verify with teeth; big penalties for wage theft, misclassification, and under‑the‑table hiring.
  - Crack down on labor brokers and traffickers, not just the workers trying to get by.

- Humanitarian lane, done responsibly:
  - Keep a steady refugee quota with tough vetting and full resettlement support—housing, English classes, job placement—spread across regions so one town isn’t overwhelmed.
  - Temporary protected status for people fleeing disasters, with regular reviews.

- A tough but workable path to get right:
  - For long‑term undocumented folks who’ve kept their noses clean: background checks, fines, taxes, English learning, then a way to earn legal status. Pair it with strict enforcement going forward so we don’t keep repeating the same mess.

- Community basics and integration:
  - Orientation on laws, safety, and local norms; English classes available and encouraged.
  - Transparency: publish local wage, hiring, housing, and school impact data so people can see what’s happening and adjust caps or support where needed.

Why this balances fairness and social integration:
- Fairness means no cutting in line, same rules for everyone, and protecting paychecks from a race to the bottom. Tying admissions to proven demand and holding employers to standards does that.
- Social integration works when change is paced and supported. Numerical limits, regional distribution, and real funding for schools and housing help communities absorb newcomers without fraying.
- It honors humanitarian values without dumping costs on the same working‑class neighborhoods already stretched.

So, my pick is job‑demand admissions plus adjustable numerical limits, backed by strong labor enforcement and real integration support. Not wide open, not slammed shut—steady, honest rules that meet needs, protect workers, and help people belong.

responses.answer:

Or when folks have different ways of doing things than what I grew up with. It makes me a bit cautious at first, maybe even unsure of how to start a conversation. I guess that’s just natural when things change fast.

Still, I think if you’re decent to people, they’re usually decent back. I try to find some common ground—ask about their garden patch, or how their kids are doing in school. You learn a lot that way. Doesn’t mean you always see eye to eye, but I’d rather try than just keep to myself.

I don’t judge; I’ve known people close to me who’ve had their own troubles. I just hope we all look out for each other. I think if you show respect and pay attention, you find ways to get along, even if everyone’s different. That’s how I see it: start with a handshake, see what happens.

The fear about jobs and wages—this one hits close to home. If you’re struggling to find work, it’s easy to worry that newcomers will make it harder. Sometimes it does, sometimes it doesn’t. I think this needs more real data, not just politicians stirring up fear. We should see the facts—who’s really getting hired, what kind of wages people are earning, and how it all fits together.

It keeps businesses going and makes sure the country runs smooth.

But there should be limits, too. You’ve got to look at how many people the country can handle without hurting local workers, driving down wages, or straining public services. I’d want policies that put Americans first when jobs are tight, but still make room for people with real skills or those fleeing real danger. We should also have strong background checks, and programs that help newcomers learn English and get used to life here—so they can fit in and not feel like outsiders forever.

So, I’d say: admit by job demand, set annual limits, have exceptions for refugees or humanitarian cases, and always pay attention to what local communities can handle. That’s the fairest way in my book—protecting American workers, keeping the country safe, but not turning our back on people who need a chance. Integration matters, too; if you’re going to live here, you should want to be part of the community, not just pass through. That’s the kind of balance I’d want.

So when I see jobs going to people who just got here... *shakes head* Look, I get that everyone's trying to make a better life for their families. I respect that. But shouldn't there be some kind of priority for people who've been paying into the system their whole lives?

I mean, my dad worked in this town for thirty years, paid his taxes, raised his kids here. I've been paying into Social Security and unemployment insurance since I was sixteen. When times get tough, shouldn't that count for something? Shouldn't the people who've been contributing get first crack at the jobs?

And it's not just about me. It's about the guy who's been doing roofing for twenty years and suddenly can't compete because someone will do it for half the wage. No benefits, no safety standards, just cash under the table. That's not fair to either worker, really.

I think fairness means taking care of your own first. Not because other people don't deserve a chance, but because that's how communities survive. You help your neighbors before you help strangers. That's just common sense.

Maybe there's room for everyone when times are good, but when resources are tight? Americans should come first in America.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character09_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*takes a deep breath, looking thoughtful*

You know, I can see truth in some of these arguments, but others... I think people are being naive.

The labor shortage thing - yeah, I get it. Nobody wants to pick strawberries or clean hotel rooms for minimum wage. But here's what bothers me: instead of raising wages to attract American workers, we just import cheaper labor. That's not solving a labor shortage, that's keeping wages low. If those jobs paid $20 an hour with benefits, you'd have plenty of Americans lining up.

The cultural diversity stuff... *shrugs* Look, I'm not against learning about other cultures. But when people talk about "vitality," what they really mean is change. And change isn't always good for the people already here. My neighborhood used to have block parties, everyone knew each other. Now it feels fragmented. Maybe that's "diverse," but it doesn't feel better.

Security concerns? That's real. I mean, we don't even know who's coming in half the time. And yeah, most people are probably decent, but it only takes a few bad actors. When you've got your own family to protect, you want to know your government is being careful about who they let in.

The humanitarian angle - I'm not heartless. If someone's genuinely fleeing for their life, that's different. But there's a difference between helping people in crisis and just letting anyone in who wants a better economic situation. We can't save everyone, and we shouldn't destroy our own communities trying.

The employment impact? *laughs bitterly* That's not a fear, that's reality. I've lived it.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character09_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*sits back, considering the options seriously*

Complete openness? That's just not realistic. You can't run a country that way - it's like leaving your front door wide open and hoping for the best. Any nation needs to control who comes in and when.

Refusing everyone? That's probably too extreme, though honestly, there are times I think we need to hit the pause button and figure out what we've got before we add more people.

If I had to choose, I'd go with numerical limits - but strict ones, and tied to what's actually good for Americans already here. Maybe some skills-based stuff, but not the way they do it now where they bring in tech workers to replace Americans for cheaper wages.

Here's what I think would be fair: First, we take care of people who are genuinely fleeing persecution - but we verify that, don't just take their word for it. Second, if there are jobs that truly can't be filled by Americans even at decent wages, then maybe we allow some workers in temporarily. But they go home when the work's done.

And integration has to mean something. Learn English. Follow our laws. Respect our customs. Don't just create little versions of wherever you came from. If you want to be American, then be American.

Most importantly, we need to enforce whatever rules we make. Right now it feels like the whole system is a joke - people ignore the law and nothing happens. That's not fair to the people who follow the rules.

*pauses* 

I know that sounds harsh to some people, but fairness means looking out for your own first. That's not racism or hatred - that's just common sense.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character09_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character09_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*pauses, the role-play ending as I transition back to being J*

You know... that was harder than I expected. Really stepping into his shoes like that, trying to speak from his heart rather than just remembering what he said.

What struck me most was how much his views came from a place of genuine fear - not hatred, but fear. Fear of losing what little stability he had, fear of his community disappearing, fear of being forgotten. When you're already struggling to keep your head above water, any change feels threatening.

I think I understood him better as a person, even if I don't agree with everything. He wasn't some cartoon villain - he was someone who felt like the world was changing around him and nobody was asking what he thought about it. That economic anxiety was so real for him.

But honestly? It also made me realize how much his perspective was shaped by... well, by only really knowing people like himself. When he talked about "community," he meant people who looked like him, grew up like him, struggled in the same ways he did. He had a hard time seeing that other people's struggles might be just as valid.

*looks thoughtful*

I guess it reminded me that behind all the political rhetoric, there are real people with real concerns. Character09_M wasn't evil - he was scared and felt unheard. But his solutions... they came from such a narrow view of what America could be.

It makes me think we need to find better ways to address that economic insecurity without... without building walls around our hearts, you know?

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character09_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to him, wasn’t about everyone getting the exact same thing—it was about playing by the same rules. He’d say, “I don’t expect a handout, and I don’t want one. But I do expect that if I show up on time, work hard, keep my nose clean, then I get a shot.” That was fairness. Not equal outcomes, but an honest chance.

He grew up in a blue-collar neighborhood where folks knew each other’s names, where you left your door unlocked and trusted your neighbor to watch your kid while you worked the second shift. Belonging, for him, meant being *seen*—not just tolerated, but known. Like when his dad got laid off from the plant, it wasn’t unemployment that kept them afloat—it was the guy down the street who slipped him cash jobs, the church ladies bringing casseroles, the union rep fighting for severance. That’s where belonging lived: in the small things people did because they considered you part of the circle.

Community, to Character09_M, wasn’t a feel-good word. It was practical. It was shared sacrifice. He used to tell this story about the winter the pipes burst in three houses on Elm Street during that cold snap ’08. No contractors came out for days—too busy, too expensive. So the guys from the neighborhood—mechanics, drywallers, even old Mr. Dern who barely walked—just showed up with tools and kettles of soup. Nobody asked permission. They just fixed it. That’s what community was: not something you talk about at meetings, but something you *do*, together.

But he also worried—quietly at first, then louder as time went on—that the circle was getting harder to define. Not because people changed, but because things shifted. Jobs moved. New faces came in. Some stayed. Some didn’t speak English. Some didn’t seem to care about the unspoken rules—the little courtesies, the quiet understandings that held things together. And he’d ask, not hatefully, but honestly: *Where do we all fit now? Can we still belong to each other when we don’t even share the same language, the same history?*

He didn’t have answers, not always. But he believed belonging had to be mutual. You had to give something to be part of something. And fairness meant making sure nobody got pushed aside—but also that newcomers didn’t skip the line he felt he’d waited his whole life in.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character09_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*[Sits back a bit, hands resting on knees, voice steady but thoughtful]*

You know, I’ve spent a lot of mornings right here in this garden. Got my plot near the back—same one for eight years now. Tomatoes, peppers, some herbs. Nothing fancy. But I come out early, not just to water, but to *see* folks.

And yeah, it’s different than it used to be. When I was a kid, most everyone on the block had dads who worked at the factory or drove trucks. Same churches, same schools, same Friday night fish fries. Now? You hear Spanish over the fence, Somali women in headscarves tending okra like they grow it back home, young gay couple from the city trying to figure out why their kale keeps dying… *[chuckles softly]* Hell, even Mrs. Langley’s got a nephew who’s non-binary now and insists on being called “they” —took me two weeks to get it right without flinching.

I won’t lie—I felt uneasy at first. Not because I’m afraid of difference, but because I didn’t know how to connect. Like when Mr. Hassan moved in next door, quiet guy, prayer rug in the window every morning. Didn’t wave at first. I thought, *Is he mad? Does he think we’re all racists?* Turned out, he just didn’t know the rhythm yet. Took six months before we shared tools. Now? He brings me dates during Ramadan. I bring him venison stew in winter. We don’t talk politics. We talk soil. Weeds. Squirrels.

But then there’s others—like that kid down the alley, always high, leaves needles in the compost bin. Or the woman with the cough who won’t go to the clinic, spreading TB like it’s nothing. That’s where it gets hard. Because I believe people deserve help—but what about the rest of us? What about fairness to those of us trying to keep things clean, safe, stable?

And look—some folks preach tolerance like it’s free. It ain’t. Tolerance costs something. It costs patience. Space. Sometimes safety. And when you’re already stretched thin—bills, job stress, kids in school—it feels like the burden keeps getting dumped on the same people: us regular Joes just trying to hold on.

Still… I can’t hate someone for being poor, or sick, or different. My granddad came from Ireland with nothing. They called him “mick,” told him to go back. He worked railroads, lived in shacks, got kicked around till he proved himself. So I get it—people want a chance.

I guess what I want is *reciprocity*. If you’re gonna live here, be part of this place, then learn the deal. Learn English. Don’t trash the common areas. Respect that we’ve been here busting our backs for generations. Join the garden. Bring something. Not just take.

Because belonging? That’s earned—not by blood or race, but by showing up. Doing your part. That’s how you become *neighbor*.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*[Leans forward, voice lower now — not angry, but firm, like he’s weighing each word]*

Look… I’ve seen addiction. My own brother nearly died from it. Lost a cousin to fentanyl. So I ain’t gonna stand here and say people struggling don’t deserve help. But there’s a difference between *helping* someone and letting their chaos spill into your life without consequence.

If the guy down the block drinks himself stupid every weekend and yells at his kids—yeah, I feel bad for the kids. But I also want him to know his behavior ain’t invisible. We don’t need sermons or judgment—we need boundaries. Say something. Knock on the door. Offer to call rehab. But don’t just shrug and say, “That’s his lifestyle.” No. When it affects others, it stops being private.

Same with disease. I had TB scare last year—turned out negative, thank God—but when that Somali woman two rows over was coughing for weeks and wouldn’t go to the clinic? That scared me. Not because she’s foreign. Because we’re all breathing the same air in this garden shed. And if public health gets ignored in the name of “respecting culture,” then who pays? People like me. The ones without good insurance, no safety net. Tolerance can’t mean silence when lives are on the line.

Now, as for race, religion, where folks come from—that’s different. That’s about dignity. My granddad was told to “go back to Ireland” in 1923. They spat on him. Called him names. So when I hear people say “go back” to immigrants today, I get sick. That shame still lives in my blood.

But—and this is where I know I’ll sound contradictory—*belonging* still means something. It ain’t enough to just *be here*. You gotta *become part of here*. I respect that Hassan prays five times a day. But if he wants his kids in the school board meeting, they better learn to speak English clear. If the lesbian couple wants to adopt, fine—love is love. But if they move in and never talk to anyone, never join clean-up day, never bring a dish to the block party—then they’re not neighbors. They’re just tenants.

And cohabiting couples? Kids born out of wedlock? Hell, half my family’s like that now. Times change. I don’t care how you live—as long as you’re not asking the rest of us to carry the cost while you break the norms.

Where I think we need more communication? With the newcomers. Not the poor ones—God bless ’em—but the ones who act like they’re entitled. Like the young tech worker who moved into the duplex, pays cash, parks in the communal spot with a “No Parking” sign, says, “I didn’t see it.” That kind of thing. That breeds resentment.

Tolerance only works both ways. I’ll accept your hijab, your pronouns, your pork-free diet—but you gotta accept mine too. My flag on the porch. My prayer before meals. My worry about jobs going to people who didn’t grow up here, didn’t serve, didn’t pay into this system.

We keep talking about “making people feel welcome.” What about making sure *everyone* feels safe? Respected? Heard?

Because comfort shouldn’t mean erasing yourself. It should mean showing up honestly—and expecting the same in return.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character09_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*[Shifts in seat, rubs the back of his neck — voice gets heavier, more worn]*

Fairness? When jobs are thin and mouths to feed are plenty… fairness means *first come, first served*—not by birth certificate, but by commitment. If you’ve paid into this place—through taxes, through time, through showing up when it was hard—then you deserve first shot when things get tight.

I worked at the warehouse for seventeen years. Not glamorous. Two shifts some weeks just to keep the heat on. And I watched guys come and go—some gave a damn, some didn’t. But every spring, same story: layoffs hit, then suddenly there’s a busload of migrant workers brought in for “seasonal help.” Next thing you know, they’re on permanent hours, living six to a trailer, sending money home, paying no local taxes, and getting benefits through loopholes I can’t even pronounce—and me? I’m begging for overtime.

Now, don’t get me wrong—I ain’t against immigrants doing honest work. Hell, my granddad was one. But back then, they came here, learned English, joined the union, stood in line like everyone else. Today? It feels like the line got erased. Like the rules changed while we were sleeping.

When jobs are scarce, fairness means protecting the people who’ve already *built* this community—the ones whose kids go to the schools, whose parents are buried in the cemetery, who showed up during floods and snowstorms. Not kicking down the door to someone else’s life because it’s cheaper.

And let’s talk about wages. I’ve seen farms, construction crews, meatpacking plants—places where locals applied, got told “we went with temporary labor.” Why? Because they’ll work for less. No health claims. No complaints. That ain’t competition—that’s exploitation. And it drags *all* of us down.

So how do I balance it?

First—*local hire first*. If you’re a citizen or legal resident who’s lived here five years, paid taxes, got clean record—you get first dibs on public projects, city contracts, any job using public money. Not forever. Just first chance. That’s fairness.

Second—*temporary worker caps*. If you bring in seasonal labor, fine. But it stays *seasonal*. No backdoor paths to permanent status unless they pay into the system like the rest of us did. No special housing, no fast-tracked benefits. Play by the same damn rules.

Third—*language and civic basics*. If you want to work here long-term, you learn English. You understand basic laws, rights, duties. Not because I hate your culture—but because this isn’t Babel. We need a common tongue to function. Otherwise, how do you report a fire? File a claim? Know your rights—or your responsibilities?

And last—*enforcement*. Not cruelty. But accountability. If an employer’s caught hiring undocumented workers to undercut wages, fine them heavy. Shut them down if they repeat. Because that ain’t business—it’s betrayal.

Look… I get that people come here for a better life. I do. But so did I. And my better life didn’t come on the back of someone else getting pushed aside.

Fairness isn’t about shutting the door. It’s about making sure the people already inside don’t get crushed trying to hold it open.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character09_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*[Leans back, takes a slow breath — voice calmer now, more reflective, like he’s sorting through real conflict inside]*

You ask me to weigh all these sides… and honestly? I don’t got a neat answer. Because the truth is, *most* of it makes some kind of sense—depending on where you’re standing.

Take the folks saying immigrants fill jobs nobody else wants. That part? I believe it. I’ve seen it. On farms, in nursing homes, in kitchens at 4 a.m.—jobs that pay too little, hurt your back, offer no future. A lot of Americans won’t take those gigs, not for what they pay. So yeah, if the work needs doing and the hands are willing, fine—let people come.

But—and there’s always a *but*—it ain’t just about filling holes. It’s about *how* they fill ’em. Are wages going down because employers know they can hire scared workers who won’t complain? Is the local hospital overwhelmed because ten families are crammed into a two-bedroom, kids getting sick, showing up in ER with no insurance? That’s not labor shortage fix—that’s cost shifting. And we’re the ones paying it.

Now, cultural diversity? Sure, adds flavor. You want good tacos, great music, new ways of thinking—immigration brings that. I’ll admit, I didn’t used to eat halal food. Now I do. My kid loves Korean pop. Fine. But don’t tell me diversity is always easy or automatically good. Not when schools have twenty languages spoken and teachers can’t teach math because half the class doesn’t understand. Not when town meetings need six translators and decisions take three times as long. Integration slows down when you don’t have common ground.

And let’s talk security. I know people roll their eyes—say it’s fear-mongering. But I remember 9/11. I remember how one guy from Saudi Arabia changed everything—fences went up, rules changed, trust vanished overnight. Doesn’t mean every immigrant’s a threat. Of course not. But it *does* mean borders matter. Screening matters. You can’t just say “open arms” and ignore that bad actors move with the flow, too. We had a guy arrested last year in Toledo—claimed asylum, worked at a plant, turned out was tied to a smuggling ring. Was he typical? No. But one’s enough to make you nervous when cops are already stretched thin.

Then there’s the humanitarian side—the refugees, the poor, the ones running from war. That gets me right here. *[Taps chest]* I saw pictures of that Syrian boy on the beach. Broke my heart. Nobody should die crossing water just to breathe free. If we’ve got room, if we can help without breaking ourselves, then yes—we should. That’s being decent.

But “room” is the key word. Where’s the room? In my town, the housing’s crumbling. Waitlists for Section 8 are three years long. Our clinic’s so backed up, I waited six weeks for a knee scan. So when a busload of asylum seekers shows up and gets placed in apartments *before* veterans or disabled locals—I get angry. Not because I hate them. Because I feel like my own people are being treated like afterthoughts.

So which views are reasonable?

- The labor argument? Reasonable—if it’s honest and temporary.
- Cultural vitality? Reasonable—if there’s effort to integrate, not just exist side by side.
- Security concerns? Reasonable—but shouldn’t become excuse for blanket suspicion.
- Humanitarian duty? Deeply reasonable—but must be balanced with capacity. Compassion without limits becomes self-destruction.

What needs more facts? The crime stats. I hear both sides. One day, “immigrants commit less crime.” Next day, “they’re overrepresented in drug rings.” Who’s right? I don’t know. I want real data—not from politicians, not from activists—but from neutral folks who just count and report. Same with wages: how much *really* does immigration pull down pay for working people? Let’s see the numbers before we shout.

And dialogue? Yeah, we need that. But not the kind where someone calls me a racist for asking questions. Or where I’m supposed to smile and say “diversity is our strength” while my neighbor’s kid can’t find a job. Real talk. Face-to-face. Not online. Not on TV. Just people—citizens, immigrants, old, young—sitting down and saying: *Here’s what I’ve lost. Here’s what I fear. Here’s what I hope.*

Because if we don’t understand each other’s pain, none of this works. Not the policy. Not the peace. Not the community.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character09_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*[Sits up straight, voice firmer now—like he’s finally getting to the point he’s been circling]*

Complete openness? No. That’s not generosity—that’s surrender. You can’t just open the door and say “come on in” when schools are overcrowded, hospitals are understaffed, and half the town’s already one paycheck from disaster. That’s not fair to anyone—including the people coming in. They deserve a system that works, not one already broken.

Refusing all foreign workers? Also no. That’s pride without sense. We’ve got aging farmers, meatpackers with back pain, nurses quitting shifts—some jobs *need* help. And if we’re honest, some Americans won’t do that work for what it pays. So shutting the door completely? That hurts the economy, the food supply, even local businesses. Stupid.

So where’s the middle?

I’d go with: **job-based admission**—but tightly controlled—and **strict numerical limits**, set every year based on real data, not politics.

Here’s how I see it:

First—**only bring in workers where there’s proven shortage**. Not “maybe we need more,” but hard evidence: X number of jobs unfilled for six months, local hiring efforts exhausted, wages rising because demand’s outpacing labor. Then—and only then—allow temporary visas for that specific job, in that sector, in that region. Farming in California? Fine. Shortage in rural nursing? Okay. But not dumping construction workers in my town when we’ve got 200 unemployed locals sitting at home.

Second—**caps based on capacity**. Not 1 million a year, not zero—something realistic. Look at housing, schools, infrastructure. If we can’t house ’em, teach ’em, or treat ’em when they’re sick, we shouldn’t be letting ’em in. Set the number low enough that integration is possible, high enough to meet actual needs. And adjust it yearly—down if times get hard, up if things improve.

Third—**temporary means temporary**. These aren’t backdoor green cards. You come for two years, you work, you pay taxes, you follow the law—you can reapply, sure, but no automatic path to citizenship. Want to stay? Go home, apply legally like everyone else. Earn it. Wait your turn.

Fourth—**integration requirements**. No exceptions. English basics before visa approval. Civics test—know the Constitution, the holidays, the laws. Not perfect fluency, but enough to function. And once here, participate: join neighborhood meetings, send kids to public school, don’t cluster in isolated pockets where no one speaks English. Integration isn’t optional. It’s the price of belonging.

Fifth—**protect local workers**. Any company hiring foreign labor has to prove they offered the job to locals first—at the same wage, same conditions. And if they’re caught paying migrants less or housing them poorly? Shut them down. Fine them heavy. Because exploitation of immigrants *hurts* American workers too—it drags wages down, kills trust, fuels resentment.

And refugees? Humanitarian cases? Small, monitored numbers—vetted thoroughly, placed where communities agree to take them, with federal support so towns like mine don’t get blindsided.

This kind of policy? It’s not flashy. Won’t win applause. But it’s fair. It says: *We’ll help—but we’re not helpless. We have limits. We have loyalty—to our people, to our history, to the folks who’ve been here busting their guts for generations.*

Fairness isn’t about being soft. It’s about being *just*. To newcomers. To taxpayers. To the guy working overtime just to keep his kid in soccer.

And social integration? That doesn’t happen by accident. It happens when rules are clear, when expectations are mutual, and when everyone knows: you’re welcome here—if you’re willing to become *part* of here.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character09_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character09_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*[Pauses for a long moment. Takes off his cap, turns it in his hands. Voice softer now — not as Character09_M, but as J, reflecting]*

Yeah… I did learn something. Not about what he believed—I already knew the bones of that. But *why* he held on so tight… I feel it more now.

When I was playing him, really trying to speak from where he stood, I realized it wasn’t just about jobs or rules. It was about dignity. About feeling like your life *mattered* in the story of this country. He never felt powerful. Never had a degree, never made big money, never got praised for anything. All he had was showing up—day after day, doing right by his family, his neighbors, his job. That was his pride.

And when everything started changing—the language, the faces, the way people seemed to move through life without roots—he didn’t see progress. He saw *erasure*. Like the world decided people like him didn’t count anymore. That their sacrifices were old news. That “fairness” now meant lifting others *over* him, instead of *with* him.

So embodying him today… it reminded me that his anger wasn’t hate. It was fear. Fear of being invisible. Of working your whole life to build something, only to be told you’re not part of the future.

And honestly? It made me question my own easy answers. I used to think, “Open the door, help where we can—that’s what good people do.” And I still believe in kindness. But I also see now that kindness without limits can feel like betrayal to those already struggling.

I won’t say I agree with every hard edge he had. Some of his suspicions… they ran deeper than facts supported. But I understand them better. They weren’t born out of cruelty—they grew from being tired. From watching friends lose jobs, towns decay, and feeling like no one in power ever listened.

This talk today… it didn’t change my politics overnight. But it restored something—his *humanity*. Not just a voice in an argument, but a man who loved this place, in his own flawed way. Who wanted fairness not because he feared others, but because he wanted to matter too.

And maybe that’s the lesson: policy isn’t just about numbers or borders. It’s about whether people feel seen. Whether they believe the game isn’t rigged against them.

If we don’t answer that—if we keep asking folks like him to sacrifice more, adjust more, accept more, without ever saying, “We see you too”—then no policy will hold. Because resentment eats community from the inside.

So thank you… for bringing him back not as a ghost, but as a teacher. Even now, he’s got something to say.
